items.question: Composition versus inheritance in a .NET microservice?
items.answer: A worker or API host is a composition root: inject IAttemptStore, ICache, and IClock through the constructor. Inheritance is for genuine is-a specialization with a stable virtual surface — like a sealed LtiHandler on an abstract AuthHandler. Deep domain hierarchies across service boundaries become versioning pain. C# allows one base class; extra roles are interfaces.
followUps: When is an abstract base still the right call?
items.sixtySeconds: Compose services with interfaces. Inherit for shared polymorphic behavior with one base. Interfaces for extra capabilities.

items.question: How does single inheritance work in C#?
items.answer: class Derived : Base is the only class inheritance shape. You get one base class plus any number of interfaces. Constructors are not inherited — Derived must call base(...) explicitly or rely on an implicit parameterless base constructor. abstract blocks instantiation; sealed blocks further derivation. Initialization order: derived field inits, base constructor body, derived constructor body.
followUps: What happens if you call a virtual method from a base constructor?
Can a struct inherit from a class?
items.sixtySeconds: One base, many interfaces. Constructors chain with base(...). Seal derived types when the set is closed.

items.question: virtual, override, abstract, sealed, and new — what does each do?
items.answer: virtual opens a dispatch slot in the method table. override replaces that slot in the derived type. abstract demands an override and forbids instantiating the type. sealed on a class blocks derivation; sealed override blocks further override and enables JIT devirtualization. new hides a member and does not participate in the base slot — calling through the base type still hits the base method. Covariant returns (C# 9+) let an override return a more derived type.
followUps: Show a bug caused by new instead of override.
What is covariant return on an override?
items.sixtySeconds: Dispatch uses the override slot. new is a different member. sealed enables devirtualization. Never call virtual from base ctor.

items.question: Explain devirtualization and when sealed matters on a hot path.
items.answer: Virtual calls walk the vtable at run time. When the JIT can prove the receiver type — sealed class, sealed override, or a local of concrete type — it may inline the target and skip the indirect call. This matters on auth handler hot paths with millions of Parse calls. It is not automatic for every virtual call; unsealed public hierarchies keep slots open. Benchmark sealed versus unsealed on the actual method before claiming a win.
followUps: Does interface dispatch devirtualize the same way?
What does BenchmarkDotNet show for sealed override?
items.sixtySeconds: Virtual is vtable dispatch. sealed lets JIT devirtualize when type is known. Measure on hot paths, do not assume every virtual call is slow.

items.question: What breaks when a base constructor calls a virtual method?
items.answer: The derived override runs before derived field initializers and constructor body complete. The override may read default/null derived fields even though the object exists. Template Method patterns in base constructors cause subtle production bugs in handler hierarchies. Fix: non-virtual hooks called from derived ctor after fields init, or a factory that calls Init() after construction.
followUps: Does primary constructor syntax change this order?
How would you spot this in a stack trace?
items.sixtySeconds: Base ctor runs before derived fields finish. Virtual call from base ctor invokes derived override on uninitialized state. Ban virtual calls in base ctors.

items.question: How do C# interfaces differ from TypeScript interfaces?
items.answer: A C# interface is a Common Language Runtime (CLR) contract: implementing types have metadata, Default Interface Methods (DIM) can run, and you can cast to the interface. TypeScript interfaces erase at compile time. Explicit interface implementation hides members unless you cast. DIM lets you add members without recompiling every implementer. Struct-to-interface conversion boxes — measure on Redis cache-key hot paths.
followUps: Can a struct implement an interface? What happens?
When do you use explicit implementation?
items.sixtySeconds: C# interfaces survive at runtime. TypeScript interfaces do not. Boxing happens when a struct is cast to an interface.

items.question: Why use a record for an auth token or Redis DTO?
items.answer: Positional records give concise immutable-shaped data, value equality, and with-expressions for nondestructive copies. Two AuthToken values with the same claims compare equal even if they are different heap objects — useful for tests and cache keys. record struct avoids a heap object when the payload is tiny. Hashing must stay consistent if you put them in dictionaries.
followUps: record versus record struct versus readonly struct?
items.sixtySeconds: Records: value equality and with. Auth and Redis DTOs fit. Equality details are the next topic.

items.question: What breaks if Equals and GetHashCode disagree?
items.answer: Dictionary, HashSet, and many caches use GetHashCode to bucket then Equals to confirm. If two objects compare equal but hash differently, lookups miss silently. If they hash equal but Equals is reference-based, you get duplicates. Mutable keys that change after insert vanish. Implement IEquatable<T> to avoid boxing value types. Records generate a consistent pair automatically.
followUps: How do records generate these methods?
Why is string a good dictionary key and a mutable DTO a bad one?
items.sixtySeconds: Hash and equals are a pair. Never mutate a key. IEquatable<T> for structs.

items.question: How is C# OOP different from JavaScript and TypeScript?
items.answer: C# types are nominal and survive as CLR metadata — casts, is checks, virtual dispatch, and access modifiers all work at runtime. TypeScript types are structural and erased — interfaces vanish in the JavaScript output. C# has real value types (struct, record struct) and a method table for virtual dispatch. JavaScript uses prototype chain lookup with no fixed virtual slots. Privacy in C# is runtime-enforced; TypeScript private is compile-time only.
followUps: Give an example of structural typing in TypeScript that C# would reject.
Does a TypeScript interface appear in a stack trace?
items.sixtySeconds: CLR keeps types. TypeScript erases them. That one fact explains every difference.
